newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela defends identity card deal with Germany.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela defends identity card deal with Germany.

text.p: The Venezuelan government brushed aside accusations on Friday of favoritism and impropriety in awarding a deal to revamp its identity card program to a German company.
"We (the government) have a totally clear and clean conscience," Interior Minister Jose Guillermo Andueza told reporters.
Opposition legislators have accused the government of accepting bribes from Germany's official press Bundesdruckerei for the contract to produce the high-tech id card system.

And lawyers representing other firms including Britain's Thomas De La Rue PLC have questioned why, after initially throwing open the contract to bidders, the government awarded it to a company which had not registered to bid and at a much higher cost than competing companies had offered.

Andueza invited regulators to investigate his accounts and rejected accusations of favoritism by stressing the benefits of awarding the contract to a state contract with a long tradition and advanced technology.
Every one of Venezuela's 22 million citizens is required to carry an id card, or cedula, even though they have to endure long lines and delays to obtain or renew them.
Venezuela hopes to replace its typewritten paper cedulas with the new plastic, digitized models before elections in December 1998.

The new cedulas will carry a hologram portrait and a tiny micro chip packed with information about the carrier. The micro chip will also make falsification also impossible, a major problem with the old cards, officials have said.
The cost of each new cedula will be $11, although this charge will only be levied if it is lost.
